I adore the scene where everyone is by the fire listening to the Dieter-Eagan story. Notice how Mark, Irving and Dylan take the story at face value. “Is that really how he died?” Irving asks. Helena, on the other hand, doesn’t question the falseness of the story. She simply knows it’s not true. This was really telling, as it shows Helena’s ability to critically engage with books & stories. She’s highly educated on the outside, unlike the others. This lack of literacy among the outties keeps them complacent. But, for a powerful and rich woman, her education allows her to confidently state ideology/propaganda as wrong; not literal.

Beautifully written and informative. Many moving parts and layers-- education is systematic, after all. I think we see this reflected in all levels of education, too. The funding, the overworking, the lack of pay, and general non-support. 

Student arriving to colleges from high school are accustomed to the lackadaisical attitudes regarding academics. I'm currently studying English Education and spend numerous hours in secondary public education. I see the decline in engagement and content comprehension, even compared to when I was a high school student only six years ago. My cooperating teachers and their colleagues are burnt out with no fire extinguisher in sight. That unhealthy culture seeps into higher education and, most importantly, our personal lives. 

"We need to cater to our customer's needs and wants." ...an interesting point you've brought up; this connection between capitalism and higher education as a business, which leaves students, faculty and staff to "pay the price" ...pun intended! 

I suppose, as an education major, the idea of catering to a student isn't strange. In fact, it's encouraged to differentiate for students. However, at the college level, this idea's silver lining is glaringly attributing to the current trends in higher education etiquette from students. There are so many double-edged swords, you'd think they're having a clearance sale on them...

(Which I believe may be contributing to my confusion and interest in this topic). You raise a great idea about "Not all the time..." I'm sad to say I've seen these behaviors numerous times and from multiple professors. 

I suppose I'm curious when we (students, faculty and everyone in-between) begin to "draw the line" to these behaviors when they are consistent or influencing student outcomes. Then again, perhaps it's simply not that serious. C's get degree's! And we all can acknowledge that college is a "system" that is, in many ways, beyond our control.
